analysis.one_liner: Lowers the minimum age to buy a handgun from a licensed dealer from 21 to 18.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 8 Republican senators including sponsor Sen. Lummis, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bars licensed gun dealers from selling handguns to anyone under 21, though 18-to-20-year-olds can legally possess handguns and buy long guns. The SAME Act would strike the 21-year minimum, letting licensed dealers sell handguns to adults 18 and older. It was introduced by Sen. Cynthia Lummis with 7 Republican cosponsors, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults aged 18 to 20 who want to buy a handgun from a licensed dealer, and licensed firearm dealers and manufacturers who gain a larger legal customer base. Supporters frame it as equal treatment for adults who can vote, serve in the military, and buy rifles at 18.

how_it_helps.text: Amends federal gun law to strike the prohibition on licensed dealers selling handguns or handgun ammunition to anyone under 21, restoring the same dealer-purchase rights for 18-to-20-year-olds that they already have for rifles and shotguns.

analysis.who_pays: No group pays a direct financial cost. The cost is in public safety risk: easier legal access to handguns — the weapon type most used in homicides and suicides — for a young-adult age group that research consistently shows is overrepresented in gun violence.

drawbacks.text: It expands handgun access for 18-to-20-year-olds, an age group that public-health research has repeatedly found to be at elevated risk of committing or dying from gun violence, which is the rationale behind the 21-year dealer rule.

It is a narrow fix: under current law 18-to-20-year-olds can already legally possess handguns and can buy them from unlicensed private sellers in most states, so the bill removes a licensing safeguard without closing the private-sale gap that critics say matters more.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to young adults is real but modest — it aligns handgun purchases with the rights they already have for long guns and removes an inconsistency in federal law. The cost is a plausible increase in handgun availability to the age band most associated with gun homicides and suicides. Whether that trade is worth making is a genuine values dispute; the bill offered no compensating safeguard, such as enhanced safety requirements, to offset the expanded access.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2021, and the committee never took it up before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cynthia Lummis introduced the SAME Act on April 27, 2021, joined by 7 Republican cosponsors: Sens. Hyde-Smith, Daines, Cramer, Braun, Crapo, and Risch.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: the federal 21-year minimum for licensed handgun sales remained in place, and 18-to-20-year-olds remained unable to buy handguns from licensed dealers. Gun dealers gained nothing; no interest group moved the needle because the bill never moved at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo and the 21-year rule

for.name: Sen. Cynthia Lummis
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wyoming, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lower the handgun purchase age to 18 and recruited 7 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 7 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.role: Original cosponsors (Hyde-Smith, Daines, Cramer, Braun, Crapo, Risch, plus sponsor Lummis)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; none of the 48 Democratic or 2 Independent senators signed on.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in April 2021 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat or Independent signed on, and the Democratic-led Judiciary Committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill would expand the legal customer base for handgun sales to include 18-to-20-year-olds, adding sales volume for dealers and makers. For the public, the same expansion means more handguns legally sold to the age group most associated with gun violence, so the industry's gain runs against the safety concern behind the current 21-year rule.
